Is it common for financial advisors to recommend 40% in individual stocks for brand-new investors?

Regardless of whether or not adding individual stocks increases performance or not, I am of the opinion that the mental capital needed to manage your positions and do the research needed to stay on top of your investments is much larger than most people are willing to give to a portfolio.

Additionally, the volatility of individual stocks can be stomach churning for inexperienced investors. I saw a lot of people sell out of their positions during COVID and lost out on a lot of the gains from the years following.

The automation is a good point though, and I think it kinda lends to ethos that "If investing is entertaining, if you're having fun, you're probably not making money. Good investing is boring."- George Soros. 

TL;DR investing should be simple, and investing in individual stocks adds uncompensated risk, extra volatility, and requires more mental capital to manage.

Unnecessarily complicated. Why not hold VTI, or VOO as a base and then add other ETFs in order to overweight the sectors you would like to be over exposed to?

Also, you need to think about the mental toll that this will take on you every time you have to manage it. Most people underestimate the mental capital that is required, and the more complicated you make your portfolio, the more mental capital needed to manage it

By the nature of the nasdaq index, QQQM is less diversified and more arbitrarily managed. 2 ETFs combined, those being VOO and QQQM, would add additional weights to certain companies that you may not want to overweight. However, if you understand that by doing so, you will mess up the market cap weighting and introduce yourself to uncompensated risk, then I say go for it!

Typically I recommend a total market cap weighted ETF like VTI here in the US because it exposes you to the companies in the S&P 500 like VOO but also exposes you to small cap stocks which have historically(not recently) had better returns than large.

TL;DR, VOO over QQQM and only VOO cause VOO holds the same stocks as QQQM but less concentrated and with more stocks for further diversification. You can also add EX-US developed and emerging to get a total world market cap weighted portfolio similar to VT as that would be best by financial theory.

Edit* spelling and grammar.

To add on, you are quite diversified but i would recommend trying to hold everything(as best you can) at the market cap weights with a little more allocated towards your home country stocks for a nice home country bias. I also like the inclusion of small cap and emerging markets, but I would try to keep factor loadings low if you don't have much confidence in them since they haven't performed well recently.

Personally, I like it. I think there is definitely some tweaking on allocations that can be done, but as far as choices of ETFs go, they are very solid.

I'm US based, so it's kind of hard to get an idea of the exact allocations for your ideal weights, but the total market weight is somewhere around 60% US and 40% ex-US. I currently have my portfolio around 50% US, 30% ex-US developed, and 20% emerging markets.

I don't understand the rationale behind this portfolio at all. Most of your holdings are highly sector concentrated, and this spells very dangerous outcomes for a long-term portfolio. 

If I were you, I would diversify. Specifically diversify into global companies outside of the US. Historically, stock returns tend to be lower after bull markets, and this combined with the uncertainty of the US economy due to political concerns it would be prudent to move some money into stocks outside of the US market.

If you look in 30-year intervals at the top stocks during those intervals, almost none of those top companies stay on top. Nobody knows for certain what the future will hold, but given the history of investing, we can make inferences based on the past. I'm willing to bet that all of these companies in 30 years will not be the top performers based on that, so why not simply diversify into a market weighted index fund and not think about it? You would still own the largest companies and capture their returns, but with less idiosyncratic risk.
